title: I vibe coded a London bus game from an idea into a playable game. Here’s what I learned
author: GeneralTobs
selftext:
I recently had the idea of turning London’s bus network into a browser game, despite not having a traditional game development team behind me.

So I decided to see how far I could take the idea using AI-assisted development.

The result is **London Red Bus**.

Players can choose London bus routes, pick up passengers, deal with traffic lights, roadworks and emergency vehicles, collect coins, compete on leaderboards and try to become King of individual routes.

AI played a significant role in helping me turn the concept into something functional, but there was still a huge amount of iteration involved: deciding what the game should actually do, testing mechanics, finding things that didn’t work, changing the experience and repeatedly refining it.

One thing this project has changed for me is how I think about the barrier between having an idea and actually shipping something people can use.

I’m curious how other AI game developers see this.  
**At what point does “vibe coding” stop being a prototype technique and become a legitimate way of building and shipping games?**

And for those who’ve shipped AI-assisted games, what problems did you only discover once real players started using them?

You can try mine here:  
[**redbus.devtalksltd.com**](http://redbus.devtalksltd.com/)

I’m particularly interested in brutal feedback on the gameplay and anything technically questionable that I should be thinking about as the player base grows.
